lines.text: Then the lights went *out.*
Emergency lights. The fans winding down.
On a space station, silence is the sound of something dying.
No hum. No fans. Just my own breathing, and my heartbeat.
Suit 2. The good one. Hale knew.
Before a spacewalk, you breathe pure oxygen for hours. Or the nitrogen in your blood fizzes, like a shaken soda.
I breathed pure oxygen for four hours, alone, in the dark, watching the oxygen fall.
And the first rule of spacewalking: never go out alone.
I had no one to go out with.
If anything went wrong out there, no one would ever know what happened.
The airlock. The hatch. And then, nothing under my feet but the Earth.
One tether. Hook, unhook, hook. Never both off.
Below me, the Earth moved at almost eight kilometers a second. A whole world every ninety minutes.
Halfway along the truss, the sun set.
The Earth below me went black, except for the cities.
The array's joint was jammed. A torn insulation blanket, wrapped around the gears.
I cut it free, piece by piece.
One wrong move with the knife, and I would cut my own suit.
My hands were shaking. Not from the cold.
And the array started to turn. Back toward the sun.
Power, 96 percent.
I breathed out for the first time in an hour.
On the way back, I passed Module 3's window.
It should have been dark.
Module 3 had been dead for a hundred and fifty days.
There was a light on in Module 3.
And a shadow *moved.*
